# Results — Study 800 (High-Frequency / Weekly Reversal)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). Recipe: each **Friday**, rank
the S&P 500 cross-section by **last week's** five-day return; long the bottom quintile
(last week's *losers*), short the top quintile (last week's *winners*), hold one week,
rebalance (Jegadeesh 1990 / Lehmann 1990, at the weekly horizon). Pinned against the
**skip-a-week bid-ask-bounce killer**, an **empirical Corwin-Schultz bounce haircut**, a
flat cost sweep with short borrow, a random-portfolio control, a beta decomposition, and a
McLean-Pontiff sub-period split. **Survivorship-biased**: the universe is the current S&P
500 projected backwards — delisted names (the very losers a reversal book would hold) are
absent, so every positive spread is an **upper bound**. As-of **2026-05-29** (the last
complete Friday of the last complete month; the in-progress week/month are dropped).
Fingerprint `e9d0f3b08c1c` (weekly total-return close panel).*

## Data stamp

| Source | Window | Shape | Fingerprint (last row) |
|--------|--------|-------|------------------------|
| Shared daily S&P 500 OHLCV panel (yfinance `auto_adjust=True`, total return) resampled to weekly `W-FRI` | 2010-01-08 → 2026-05-29 | 856 weeks × 500 tickers | `e9d0f3b08c1c` |

Universe: ~476 names with a valid weekly close in a given week; ~95 per quintile. Weekly
effective spread is the mean daily **Corwin-Schultz (2012)** high-low estimate within each
week (median **44 bps** — an upper-bound liquidity proxy that carries the *relative* fact
that losers are less liquid than winners).

## The headline — the loser-minus-winner weekly spread

| Portfolio | Return | HAC *t* |
|-----------|--------|---------|
| **Loser quintile**  | **+24.4%/yr** | **+4.99** |
| Winner quintile     | +15.3%/yr     | +3.73     |
| **Spread (Loser − Winner), skip=0** | **+17.5 bps/wk = +9.1%/yr** | **+2.47** |

Hit-rate 456/854 weeks = 53.4% (Wilson 95% [50.0%, 56.7%]). The raw weekly spread **clears
the desk bar of |t| = 2** — last week's losers *do* beat last week's winners next week. So
far, so promising. Then the honest checks dismantle it.

## Killer #1 — the bid-ask-bounce test (skip a week)

| Variant | Spread | HAC *t* |
|---------|--------|---------|
| skip=0 (last week's close **forms** the signal *and* **prices** the entry) | +17.5 bps/wk | **+2.47** |
| **skip=1 (one-week gap before holding)** | **−1.7 bps/wk** | **−0.28** |

Inserting a single week between the formation close and the holding week **annihilates**
the effect (*t* falls from +2.47 to **−0.28** — an outright sign flip to zero). A reversal
that lives only when last week's *close* both forms the signal and prices the entry is the
textbook **bid-ask-bounce illusion** (Jegadeesh 1990; Lehmann 1990; Lo-MacKinlay 1990): a
name that closed on the bid prints a low return and "reverts" upward purely because the
next print lands on the ask. Measured one week out, the tradable component is **gone**.

## Killer #2 — the empirical Corwin-Schultz bounce haircut

Each leg pays its **own** estimated effective spread (losers are illiquid and pay more than
winners), scaled by the fraction of the leg turned over that week; the short leg also pays
50 bps/yr borrow.

| Spread crossed | Net spread | Net HAC *t* |
|----------------|------------|-------------|
| half-spread | **−28.8 bps/wk** | **−4.29** |
| full-spread | **−74.2 bps/wk** | **−11.46** |

Even charging only *half* the estimated roundtrip spread, the book is deeply loss-making —
the raw +17.5 bps is smaller than the cost of crossing the losers' own bid-ask spread.

## Tradability — flat cost sweep and break-even

The loser and winner legs each turn over **~78% one-way every week** (a one-week signal is
almost entirely refreshed at each rebalance). Costs are one-way × NAV across both legs,
round-trip; the short pays 50 bps/yr borrow.

| One-way cost | Net spread | Net HAC *t* |
|--------------|------------|-------------|
| 0 bps  | +16.6 bps/wk | +2.34 |
| 5 bps  | +0.9 bps/wk  | +0.13 |
| 10 bps | −14.8 bps/wk | −2.10 |
| 20 bps | −46.1 bps/wk | −6.61 |

**Break-even flat one-way cost: ~5.6 bps.** A weekly-rebalanced small-cap-tilted long-short
book cannot be run at 5.6 bps all-in; by 10 bps it is significantly loss-making. Combined
with the skip=1 collapse, the gross spread is a measurement artefact long before it is a
trade.

## Beta decomposition and the random-portfolio null

| Leg | Beta vs EW market | Alpha (ann) |
|-----|-------------------|-------------|
| **Spread (dollar-neutral), skip=0** | **+0.293** | **+3.83%/yr** |

The dollar-neutral spread is near market-neutral (beta 0.29) — so the raw effect is *not*
disguised beta; it is genuine cross-sectional structure. The problem is not beta, it is
**microstructure and decay**. A random quintile of the loser-leg size, drawn 60×/week
(51,240 draws), has mean excess **+0.11 bps** — centred at zero, confirming any loser
excess is signal, not concentration.

## Post-publication decay (McLean-Pontiff)

| Period | Spread (skip=0) | HAC *t* | n weeks |
|--------|-----------------|---------|---------|
| 2010-2015 | +25.9 bps/wk | **+4.00** | 310 |
| 2016-2020 | +23.4 bps/wk | +1.22 | 261 |
| 2021-2026 | **+2.9 bps/wk** | **+0.26** | 283 |

The entire full-sample *t* is carried by the early 2010s. Since ~2021 even the *raw*
skip=0 spread is indistinguishable from zero — the electronic-market-making and stat-arb
competition that killed the monthly reversal (study 329) has reached the weekly horizon too.

## Synthetic positive control — the machinery is faithful

Deterministic, no network. The engine must (a) stay quiet on the null, (b) keep a **real**
reversal alive through a one-week skip, and (c) let a **pure bid-ask bounce** die at skip=1.

| World | skip=0 *t* | skip=1 *t* |
|-------|-----------|-----------|
| null (reversal = bounce = 0), **12 seeds** | mean **−0.64** (\|t\|≥2 in 0/12) | mean −0.26 |
| planted real reversal (0.5) | **+16.22** | **+20.99** — SURVIVES |
| planted pure bid-ask bounce (0.008) | **+10.71** | **−1.35** — DIES |

The skip test keeps a genuine reversal and destroys a pure bounce — exactly what it does to
the real tape (skip=0 +2.47 → skip=1 −0.28, the *bounce* signature). *(A faithful-engine /
power check only — never cited in support of the real-tape stamp.)*

## Verdict

- **Signal — WEAK.** The raw weekly spread clears the bar (skip=0 HAC *t* = +2.47, and it
  is near-market-neutral, beta 0.29) — so there *is* a real, measurable short-horizon
  reversal on the tape. But it is **not robust**: a one-week skip removes 100% of it
  (*t* = −0.28), and even the raw effect has decayed to zero since ~2021 (*t* = +0.26). A
  signal that survives only when the same close forms and prices the trade is not a real
  edge — it is bid-ask bounce. Survivorship-biased upper bound throughout.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** ~78% weekly one-way turnover on each leg; break-even ~5.6 bps
  flat; the empirical Corwin-Schultz bounce haircut is −28.8 bps/wk even at half-spread. A
  weekly-refreshed book of a signal that already evaporates one week out cannot be traded.
- **Is it bid-ask bounce? — CONFIRMED.** The one-week skip removes the entire effect, and
  charging each leg its own spread turns it deeply negative.
